p: On Christmas Day in the year eight hundred, in the old basilica of Saint Peter at Rome, as the king of the Franks rose from prayer, Pope Leo the Third placed a crown upon his head, and the people cried out, to Charles, crowned by God, great and peace-giving emperor of the Romans, life and victory. Charles, whom we call Charlemagne, from the Latin Carolus Magnus, meaning Charles the Great, told his biographer afterwards that had he known what the pope intended, he would not have entered the church that day, even though it was a great feast. Historians have argued ever since whether to believe him. Men who are surprised by crowns have generally been thinking about them for some time.

The Franks were a Germanic people who had settled in Gaul as the western empire collapsed, and whose king Clovis had become a Catholic Christian about the year five hundred, a choice that won him the support of the Roman bishops and the Roman population. Charlemagne, born about seven hundred and forty-seven, was the grandson of Charles Martel, who had turned back the Arabs near Tours, and the son of Pepin, who had made himself king with the blessing of the pope. He reigned for forty-six years, and for almost every one of them he was at war. He conquered the Lombards of northern Italy, and took their iron crown. He fought the Saxons of north Germany for thirty years and forced them into Christianity at the point of the sword, beheading, on a single day at Verden, some four and a half thousand who had rebelled; it is the darkest stain upon his memory. He destroyed the Avars of the Danube. He campaigned in Spain, and the destruction of his rearguard in the passes of the Pyrenees, in seven hundred and seventy-eight, by Basques, became, in the Song of Roland, a legend of heroic war against the Saracens. By the end of his reign he ruled most of western Christendom: what is now France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Switzerland, most of Germany and half of Italy.

He was a big man, by his biographer Einhard's account, with a high voice and a fondness for swimming and for roast meat, which his physicians forbade him in vain. He spoke Latin and understood Greek. He tried to learn to write in his old age, keeping tablets under his pillow to practise in the night, but began too late, and never mastered it. This unlettered king was nevertheless the greatest patron of learning in the West since the fall of Rome. He gathered scholars to his court at Aachen from all over Europe, the chief of them an Englishman, Alcuin of York. He ordered that every monastery and cathedral should keep a school. His scribes developed a new, clear handwriting, with small letters, now called Carolingian minuscule, and copied the works of the ancient Latin authors with great care. Most of the ancient Latin literature we possess survives because it was copied in the monasteries of his empire. When, six centuries later, the scholars of the Italian Renaissance looked for the clear handwriting of the ancients, they found it in these Carolingian manuscripts, and imitated it, believing it Roman; and from their imitation come the letters of our printed books. You are, in a sense, reading Charlemagne whenever you read a newspaper.

His empire did not survive his grandsons, who divided it among themselves in eight hundred and forty-three, roughly into a western kingdom that became France, an eastern kingdom that became Germany, and a middle kingdom that has been fought over by the other two ever since, as the late war of eighteen seventy has reminded us. But the idea of a Christian empire in the West, allied to the pope, lasted as the Holy Roman Empire for another thousand years, until Napoleon abolished it in eighteen hundred and six.

Even in Charlemagne's lifetime, a new terror had appeared on the coasts. In the year seven hundred and ninety-three, raiders from Scandinavia fell upon the monastery of Lindisfarne, on its island off the coast of Northumberland, killed the monks, and carried off its treasures. Alcuin wrote from the Frankish court in horror that never before had such terror appeared in Britain. It was the beginning of the Viking age, which lasted for some two and a half centuries.

The Vikings, as we now call them, a name whose origin is uncertain, came from Norway, Denmark and Sweden. Their advantage was the ship: long, light, shallow, with sails and oars, able to cross the North Sea and also to row far up rivers. They raided monasteries because monasteries were rich and undefended. But they were not only raiders. They were traders, carrying furs, slaves and amber, and they were settlers. They took the north and east of England, where the Danish law and many Danish place names, those ending in by and thorpe, survive, and were held back only by Alfred, king of Wessex, the only English king to be called the Great. They settled in Ireland and founded Dublin. In France, a Viking chief named Rollo was granted the land at the mouth of the Seine in nine hundred and eleven, and his descendants, the Normans, became French in speech and conquered England in ten sixty-six. The Swedes went east, down the rivers of Russia to the Black Sea and Constantinople, where the emperors employed them as a bodyguard, and founded the state of the Rus, from which Russia takes its name.

Most remarkably, they sailed west across the open Atlantic: to the Faroe Islands, to Iceland, settled from about eight hundred and seventy, where they founded a commonwealth governed by an assembly of free men and wrote the great prose stories called the sagas; to Greenland, under Erik the Red; and, about the year one thousand, to a land beyond, which they called Vinland. It was long thought a legend. The Encyclopaedia reports that in nineteen sixty a Norse settlement was found at a place in Newfoundland called L'Anse aux Meadows, a name which seems to come from an old French one meaning the cove of jellyfish, which proves that Norsemen reached America nearly five hundred years before Columbus. They did not stay. America, it seems, was not yet ready to be discovered, or the discoverers were not yet ready to keep it.
